A generic 4-vertex has two branches meeting at the flat state; around a loop the fourth vertex is over-determined, so most branch assignments have energy of order κρ⁴ and the sheet's landscape is glassy, with distractor branches growing as 2^(α√A), α ≈ 2.25. Folding is zero-temperature descent, so randomly placed actuators usually misfold the sheet: 18 of 60 creases on one 4 × 4 pattern for a 50% chance. Whether the union of the actuated creases' folding islands covers the sheet predicts success better than the number of actuators, and an added actuator with a small island can ruin a successful folding. The difficulty is at the flat state. | Read |
| [NOTE-1574](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1574.md) | Chen, Choi & Mahadevan — Deterministic and stochastic control of kirigami topology | Quad kirigami as a linkage. Exact minimum link counts: δ(L) = ⌈(3L²−3)/2⌉ to rigidify an L × L sheet, γ(L) = L² − 1 to connect it, proved by construction, so rigidifying always needs more links and no pattern is minimal for both; random choice almost never finds either. With random links, the maximum of internal DoF (ρ_i ≈ 0.26), connectivity percolation (ρ_c ≈ 0.293, 1 − 1/√2 analytically) and a rigidity transition (ρ_r ≈ 0.429) fall in that order; each link changes the total DoF, changes the internal DoF, or is redundant. Planar, infinitesimal rigidity, no experiments. | Read |
| [NOTE-1580](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1580.md) | Hopkins — Hybrid flexure systems and elements via Freedom and Constraint Topologies | Restates FACT and extends it to hybrid flexures: parallel limbs, each serial or hybrid, and flexure elements with no intermediate rigid bodies. Freedom and constraint spaces are reciprocal, with 6 − n independent wrenches and 50 types; in parallel, constraint spaces add and freedom spaces intersect, in series the reverse. Summing the elements' orders of constraint against the system's constraint space tests for exact and over-constraint, and freedoms left in intermediate bodies mark under-constraint, which costs vibration and controllability. Ten hybrid elements are given. Kinematic only; no interconnected limbs. | Read |
| [NOTE-1582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1582.md) | Krishnakumar and Suresh — Hinge-free compliant mechanisms by the topological level-set | Compliant-mechanism topology optimization trades flexibility at the output against stiffness against a workpiece. The authors maximize mutual strain energy over a weighted sum of input and output strain energies and remove material by the topological derivative of that ratio, so elements are only in or out: no pseudo-densities, no point hinges, well-conditioned stiffness matrices, and a sequence of designs of falling volume in one run. Raising the weight η raises geometric and lowers mechanical advantage. Linear elasticity, coarse meshes, no fabrication. | Read |
| [NOTE-1587](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1587.md) v2 | Evans, Silverberg & Santangelo — Lattice mechanics of origami tessellations | A lattice theory of periodic origami. Each degree-N vertex has N − 3 internal degrees of freedom with several configuration branches. Vertices are joined through shared folds, and a Bloch-wave ansatz gives a rigidity-like matrix. In the Miura-ori, with facet bending as extra folds, three uniform zero modes are bulk modes. The inhomogeneous soft modes are localized at the edges with an analytic decay length, checked on an 8 × 8 paper sheet with an indenter and with reversible pop-through defects, and the degrees of freedom scale with the perimeter. Linear, one ground state. It does not state the 2014 paper's bistable cells or crystal-defect analogy. Read in full; the step to the decay length is checked. | Read |
| [NOTE-1588](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1588.md) v2 | Connelly and Whiteley — Second-order rigidity and prestress stability for tensegrity frameworks | For frameworks of bars, cables and struts, first-order rigidity implies prestress stability, which implies second-order rigidity, which implies rigidity, and examples show none of these reverses, even for bar frameworks. Whether a first-order flex extends to second order is decided by a Farkas-type test over all the proper self-stresses; with a one-dimensional cone of flexes or of stresses, second-order rigidity and prestress stability coincide. Read: the hierarchy's proofs and the stress test's; the later applications (§§5.4–5.6) were skipped. | Read |
| [NOTE-1592](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1592.md) v2 | Hopkins — Parallel flexure design via Freedom and Constraint Topologies (master's thesis) | The founding statement of FACT for parallel flexures. Motions are twists, constraints wrenches, and the freedom space is the null space of the constraint wrenches; each freedom space is linked one to one with a constraint space, and for ideal pure-force constraints the pairs fall into 26 types in six cases. A redundant constraint is one whose addition or removal leaves the freedom space unchanged while stiffness, load capacity and stability change, and the design procedure uses such constraints for stiffness and symmetry. Some motion sets cannot be had from constraints without unwanted extra freedoms. Elastomechanics, dynamics and actuation are out of scope. | Read |
| [NOTE-1596](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1596.md) v2 | Hopkins — Flexure motion stages via Freedom, Actuation and Constraint Topologies (PhD thesis) | Extends FACT from parallel to serial flexures and from kinematics to actuation. With constraints of any pitch there are 50 freedom/constraint space types; only those inside a "parallel pyramid" can be built in parallel, and the rest need modules stacked in series, whose freedoms add. A serial system whose intermediate bodies keep freedoms is underconstrained and has poor dynamics. A twist–wrench stiffness matrix gives the actuation space, where linear actuators must act to drive the freedoms without parasitic error; it depends on the flexures' geometry and material, so the freedom space alone does not fix it (implied, not said). One experiment located the least-error actuator line near the predicted one. The 50 rest on a case analysis (App. A) that defers to the master's thesis for the 2-DOF column and the column symmetry. | Read |
| [NOTE-1597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1597.md) | Kinoshita and Ohsaki — Bistable compliant frames converted from truss mechanisms | A bistable compliant truss mechanism, found by an earlier optimization, is converted into a single-piece frame by replacing each pin joint with a pseudo-joint of thin end regions and optimizing their area and length ratios (OPT2) to keep the output displacement and a second self-equilibrium state, under a strain cap that prevents a point hinge. In the one example the frame keeps the second equilibrium, with the largest thin-element strain at 0.99 of the cap. Computational, one example, no fabrication. | Read |
| [NOTE-1600](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1600.md) | Liu, Fang, Xu and Wang — Multistable origami metamaterials for mechanical learning | A stacked Miura-origami metamaterial of bistable cells, driven by a fixed sequence of tension and compression, serves as the reservoir of a reservoir computer, with a trained linear readout of its visited configurations. In experiment a 4×2-cell prototype recognizes ten 5×4-pixel digits; in simulation MNIST reaches 90.4% against 87.2% without the reservoir, and a retained buffer zone carries input history on a 5-bit memory task. An all-compression rule erases inputs. | Read |
| [NOTE-1601](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1601.md) | Kane and Lubensky — Topological boundary modes in isostatic lattices | In isostatic lattices the zero-mode count of a region is a local count of sites and bonds plus a topological count fixed by winding numbers of the bulk equilibrium matrix. Gapped phases of different topological polarization therefore carry floppy modes, or states of self-stress, at their edges and domain walls where constraints and freedoms locally balance. Shown in a 1D rotor chain (the SSH model) and a deformed kagome lattice; linear theory, needing a bulk gap and a gauge choice of unit cell. | Read |
| [NOTE-1605](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1605.md) | Berry, Lee-Trimble and Santangelo — Vertex curvature and the topology of origami configuration space | Extends Chen and Santangelo's second-order theory to origami whose vertices carry Gaussian curvature K. The vertex condition becomes hᵀQh = K; with one negative eigenvalue in Q, a vertex with small K > 0 has its two nappes (popped up, popped down) in disconnected components near the flat state, and one with K < 0 has them joined by a neck, given that faces may not pass through each other. Degree-4 vertices are split for both signs. The multi-vertex extension is conditional, and the suggestion that curvature can prevent misfolding is deferred to future work. | Read |
| [NOTE-1607](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1607.md) | Rocks et al. — Allostery-inspired response tuned into spring networks by bond removal | Of the arXiv preprint. In disordered spring networks, greedy removal of about 1% of bonds (2D) or 0.5% (3D), each chosen with an analytic update from the states of self-stress and compatible stress, tunes a chosen source-to-target strain ratio to within 1%, failing in under 2% (2D) and 1% (3D) of networks for \|η\| up to 1; several targets from one source, and two independent pairs, are tuned too. Four physical realizations match simulation at C = 0.98 ± 0.02. Linear, athermal, central forces; why particular bonds work is left open. | Read |
| [NOTE-1608](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1608.md) | Hu, Tan, Chen and Yan — Spatially programmable origami networks for mechanical computing | Flat-foldable origami switches make Buffer and NOT elements; a gate of two is turned from AND to OR by rotating them from series to parallel, and a Rubik's-cube arrangement changes the sum-of-products function its columns compute by permuting elements. A 30-gate array realizes four 2-bit functions; a third-order cube switches between full adder and full subtractor; a second-order cube, rotated by a servo, drives a robot's path decisions. Inputs are mechanical; outputs and inter-gate signals are electrical. | Read |
| [NOTE-1614](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1614.md) | Chen and Santangelo — Branches of triangulated origami near the unfolded state | A second-order rigidity theory for flat triangulated rigid origami. Each self stress of the flat sheet gives a quadratic constraint on vertex heights; the wheel stress of an internal vertex is exactly preservation of its zero Gaussian curvature, so one vertex's near-flat configurations form a double cone (popped up, popped down). For four-boundary-vertex patterns, numerics on random triangulations find 2^Vi branches at the flat state, two per vertex sign pattern up to global sign, proven for H1 triangulations. The self-folding consequence: misfolding is likely, and driving forces orthogonal to all wrong branches cannot be had. | Read |
| [NOTE-1615](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1615.md) | Stern et al. — Supervised training of a creased sheet by crease-stiffness plasticity | Of the arXiv preprint. A model creased sheet is trained by folding it under example force patterns and changing each crease's stiffness by a local rule, softening if a supervisor judges the fold correct and stiffening if not. It then folds unseen patterns into the right class's structure, about 80% on spherical-cap classes and 91% on two Iris species, because the acquired stiffness heterogeneity cuts the number of accessible folded structures and enlarges the survivors' attractors; overtraining leaves one structure. Simulation only. | Read |
| [NOTE-1616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1616.md) | Mirth et al. — Energy landscapes by sublevelset persistent homology | Sublevelset persistent homology of a potential energy landscape: its zero-dimensional barcode carries the disconnectivity graph, and its higher-dimensional bars record transition paths the graph omits and, for a Morse function, critical points of every index. For the alkane torsional landscape on the n-torus the barcode is proved in closed form in every dimension; barcode distances compare analytical and MD-sampled landscapes and grow where sampling is poor. | Read |
| [NOTE-1617](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1617.md) | Jules et al. — Delicate memory structure of origami switches | Four bistable Kresling barrels of different pattern angle, stacked in series and loaded uniaxially with ends clamped against rotation, form a Preisach memory: all 16 states are stable and reachable, the transition graph is fixed by the order of the switching thresholds, and it shows return-point memory. Twisting by hand reaches defect states the boundary conditions should forbid; they are unreachable from the main graph, grouped in strongly connected loops, and left only by irreversible erasure or shift of the defect. Height and stiffness identify states only partly. | Read |
| [NOTE-1619](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1619.md) | Kang, Kim, Yang and Ryu — Physics-informed neural networks for programmable origami | A network of two 128-unit tanh layers maps the height of a conical Kresling cell to its twist and is trained without data on the energy of a truss model along the torque-free path; trained jointly with the geometry, it inverts the energy curve from two stable heights and a barrier. Agreement with a beam-truss FEA is high; a three-layer stack with ascending barriers folds in order in FEA and in one PET prototype, with barrier errors of −7.93% and −16.16% after normalizing to the bottom layer. | Read |
| [NOTE-1624](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1624.md) | Chen et al. — Topological mechanics of origami and kirigami | Marginally rigid origami and kirigami carry a topological polarization. A zig-zag origami strip folds at the edge its pattern angles select, with decay rate ln κ, confirmed in Mylar experiments; linear analysis fails at the flat state, where coplanar hinges are redundant constraints. Periodic triangulated origami appears always to have zero polarization (conjectured on numerics), but kirigami can be polarized, and a domain wall between kirigami of different polarizations is flexible amid rigid regions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1625](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1625.md) | Lee Tin Wah et al. — Observing and controlling the folding pathway of DNA origami | AFM snapshots of Rothemund's tall rectangle, adsorbed out of solution along a slow cooling ramp, show folding nucleating at the top and bottom ends between about 65 and 55 °C and growing inward; raising the central staples and cutting the edge staples moves nucleation to the centre with no change of sequence. The authors argue thermodynamic control by the staples' melting temperatures. One design; the two concentration changes made together; no yield under the altered condition. | Read |
| [NOTE-1626](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1626.md) v2 | Cumberworth and Reinhardt — Models and simulations of structural DNA nanotechnology | Read in full. In the review's account of simulations, a staple's later domains bind within one structure without a second translational penalty, but each loop closed constrains the scaffold at an entropic cost that depends on binding order; small loops tend to close first, and a staple typically binds fully once started. Origami assembly is mostly downhill and needs no nucleation barrier, unlike DNA bricks, though one can be designed in; blocking is rare at typical staple concentrations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1627.md) | Shirt-Ediss, Torelli et al. — Optimising DNA origami assembly by reducing off-target interactions | For four DNA origami shapes (2D triangle and rectangle, 3D tetrahedron, 6-helix bundle), three scaffold sequences each, with fully complementary staples, were chosen by four off-target binding scores and folded under one protocol. The sequences scored most prone to off-target binding gave only 0–20% well-folded objects under AFM and aggregated, the Pareto-front Lambda sequences always did better, and a de Bruijn control was best except for the rectangle in the replication. The link is correlational, three variants per shape; the authors attribute the failures to kinetic trapping, which is not observed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1628](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1628.md) | Zhou et al. — Mutations in artificial self-replicating tiles | Two cross-tile origami dimer species each template their own kind from supplied monomers; three mismatched bases in 42 make about 3.5% of AB's copies CD. With equal growth rates (3.7 and 3.9 per cycle) the species converge toward equal shares; with AB held to at most 2 per cycle, the mutant CD reaches parity within five cycles and dominates after nine. Growth rate, set by the recognition-strand design, is the only fitness, and monomers, temperatures and UV are supplied every cycle. | Read |
| [NOTE-1629](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1629.md) | Douglas et al. — Self-assembly of DNA into nanoscale three-dimensional shapes | Origami extended to multilayer 3D solids on a honeycomb lattice, with design rules and a one-pot fold at 7–44 % of scaffold in monomer, but only with week-long ramps at about 16 mM MgCl2 and low NaCl; short ramps, low Mg2+ or high Na+ give grossly misshapen products, while flat and six-helix-bundle origami fold in 72 minutes. Mechanisms, kinetic traps included, are conjecture; the Supplementary Information unread. | Read |
| [NOTE-1630](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1630.md) | Ni et al. — Cooperativity, entropy, and effective concentration in DNA origami self-replication | In a cross-tile self-replication cycle, a seed of origami tiles recruits supplied monomer tiles, whose tethered horizontal sticky ends, at an effective concentration raised from about 1 nM to about 0.8 mM, melt about 50 °C higher than in solution; UV fixes them and heating separates daughter from parent. A two-state model with three entropy terms, fitted once, predicts the melting of 1- to 4-tile assemblies to about 2 °C. Replication rates fall from about 1.9 per cycle for dimers to 1.6 for tetramers, and tetramers barely separate before the tiles unravel. | Read |
| [NOTE-1631](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1631.md) | Rothemund — Folding DNA to create nanoscale shapes and patterns | One long scaffold strand, raster-routed through a shape, is pinned by about 200–250 staples designed to bind only the scaffold; one anneal of about two hours folds six shapes about 100 nm across. Yields of well-formed structures, judged in AFM fields, run from about 1% to 90% by design. Staple excess matters only near 1:1. AFM resolves single missing staples only under conditions that damage the sample. The mechanism offered, strand invasion and cooperative staple binding, is argued, not tested. | Read |
| [NOTE-1632](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1632.md) | Majikes et al. — Thermodynamics of a single DNA origami fold via affine transformations | A single-fold DNA origami model with a FRET reporter, melted in replicate and baseline-corrected by affine curve collapse: closing a fold is unimolecular and more stable than bimolecular binding of the same domain, and its melting temperature falls with fold distance by more than 10 °C from short to long, through loop entropy; ΔCp is not negligible. The authors infer, untested, that origami folds by nucleation and growth. One fold, melt ramp only, no hysteresis or kinetics; the supplement unread. | Read |
| [NOTE-1633](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1633.md) | Majikes et al. — The blocked state as a limit on single-fold yield in DNA origami | A single-fold origami assay with a topology reporter finds that the folded fraction after annealing rises with staple excess to a turnover near 1–5× and then falls below 50 %, because each of a staple's two scaffold domains can be taken by a separate staple (the blocked state), as an equilibrium model with folded/blocked = j_fold/[staple] predicts; motif does not matter and a twofold slower anneal gives the same trend. The whole-origami escape by cooperativity and strand displacement is proposed, not tested; the supplement unread. | Read |
| [NOTE-1634](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1634.md) | Douglas, Bachelet and Church — A logic-gated DNA origami nanorobot | A DNA-origami barrel fastened by two aptamer locks opens, as an entropic spring, only when both antigen keys bind: a logical AND gate over cell-surface inputs, its rule fixed at fold time by the aptamer sequences, its key sensitivity set by lock length (10 pM for 16–23 bp, 1 nM for 30–44 bp, shorter locks opening spontaneously more often). Guide staples raise the closed-state yield from 48 % to 97.5 %. The device carries a rule it cannot revise; the Supporting Online Material unread. | Read |
| [NOTE-1635](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1635.md) | Marras et al. — Programmable motion of DNA origami mechanisms | DNA origami sliders and hinges built from stiff bundles joined only by single-stranded scaffold move in one designed degree of freedom whose range and stiffness the connection lengths set; TEM fluctuations, Boltzmann-inverted, give the force or torque to hold each configuration. A crank–slider and a Bennett linkage follow their rigid-body paths; the linkage's higher-energy compacted state, rarely occupied unaided, is held by locking staples or closing strands and released by strand displacement, each move in about a minute. TEM on a surface, small samples, misfolds excluded, SI unread. | Read |
| [NOTE-1636](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1636.md) | Scheckenbach et al. — Self-regeneration and self-healing in DNA origami | DNA origami repaired from strands in solution, in two modes the authors separate. Self-regeneration: weakly bound 13-nt labels turn over against a 5 nM pool and recover after bleaching, fully when photostabilized. Self-healing: free staples enter only where a toehold is exposed, so a matching staple pool keeps 76% of nanorulers intact over 11 days in 0.2% serum against 12% without, and fails to beat non-matching DNA in 10% serum. A 12HB missing nine staples is half repaired by an anneal from 50 °C. The scaffold cannot be repaired. | Read |
| [NOTE-1637](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1637.md) | Wagenbauer, Wachauf and Dietz — Quantifying quality in DNA self-assembly | Negative-stain TEM averages and gel mobility cannot tell a 42-helix bundle with all its staples from one missing 5 or 15 of 207. A fluorescent de Bruijn probe for unpaired bases, read on a cold gel and calibrated by deliberate omissions, can, and it finds 1.2 to 6.2 staple equivalents missing in complete reactions by design. Used on folding protocols, it finds a design-dependent isothermal optimum and a short stepped schedule matching a 16-hour ramp that hours at one temperature do not. | Read |
| [NOTE-1638](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1638.md) | Cumberworth, Frenkel and Reinhardt — Design-dependent nucleation barriers in DNA origami | Monte Carlo free energies of a domain-level lattice model of one scaffold in staples at constant chemical potential, for four small planar designs. Designs S, D and two-row assemble downhill; three-row, with three-domain staples, has a barrier of about 10 kBT at Tm (about 20 kBT at domain resolution) that is gone a few degrees below. Stacking between adjacent staples switches the barrier on and off; hybridization strength barely moves it. Equilibrium only: no kinetics, yields or simulated hysteresis. | Read |
| [NOTE-1639](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1639.md) | Majikes et al. — Complex cooperativity in DNA origami revealed via design-dependent defectivity | 34 designs of one 2D origami rectangle, annealed fast at 0.375 nM with 5x staples so defects are common, imaged by liquid AFM and classed into four classes, give a defectivity φ of about 10 to 35, with staple-pool variation (±2.8) the largest uncertainty. Defectivity tracks the skew of the first-fold loop-entropy penalty distribution and the measured melt temperature; with a blocking metric, roughly equal weights collapse it onto one trend over 28 designs. Designs with more short folds at the expense of medium ones did worse. The authors read 2D origami assembly as funnel-like rather than path-like. | Read |
| [NOTE-1640](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1640.md) | Winfree and Bekbolatov — Proofreading tile sets | In kTAM simulation and kinetic-trap theory, direct tile sets err because a mismatched tile is covered before it can leave, giving r ≈ βε². A K×K block with unique internal labels keeps the logical (aTAM) assembly, scaled by K, but makes any single mismatch a dead end, so growth stalls until it dissociates: 2×2 gives r ≈ βε and errors 1% → 0.01% at fixed conditions; 3×3 only 0.001%, short of the predicted exponential gain, because growth on facets is not corrected. Proofreading tiles heal punctures, with less scar tissue than direct ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-1641](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1641.md) | Schneider, Möritz and Dietz — The sequence of events during folding of a DNA origami | One 42-helix honeycomb origami brick (140 staples, 5880 bp) folded at 50 °C in 20 mM MgCl2 after a 65 °C step, with every staple's incorporation tracked by beacon and FRET assays in qPCR machines. Staple termini bind independently; binding strength barely predicts order; a scaffold permutation with new sequences and the same connectivity keeps the order; removing the earliest segments abolishes a compacted intermediate and delays folding by hours through a slower pathway. Long-range crossovers join co-folding clusters, read as nuclei. | Read |
| [NOTE-1642](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1642.md) | Aksel et al. — Design principles for accurate folding of DNA origami | Staple breakpoints of a caDNAno design are chosen by a k-shortest-path search over a weighted graph whose edge weights come from an equilibrium free energy (binding, loop closure, hybridization) at 50 °C. Four published multilayer blocks so redesigned rose in gel-measured accurate-folding yield from 2-6% to 48-61% after one 21 h anneal, three with the same scaffold route and helix layout, and yields correlate with the model's score (R² = 0.86, 8 designs). The score ignores kinetics and inter-staple cooperativity; yield is one hand-bounded gel window. | Read |
| [NOTE-1643](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1643.md) | Dunn et al. — Guiding the folding pathway of DNA origami | A dimer origami template with about 10^23 staple configurations and 6 distinguishable well-folded shapes of roughly equal free energy is annealed once (95 to 25 °C at 1 °C per minute), and AFM shape counts report which pathway was taken. Weakening the cooperative long-range seam staples shifts products toward the fold short-range staples favour; extended short-range staples suppress another fold; two further variants steer by final-state stability instead. A domain-level kinetic model matches three of four variants and puts misfolds at 52% with full seams and 1% with broken ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-1644](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1644.md) v2 | Sobczak — Investigations of the DNA origami folding process (dissertation) | Gel and SYBR Green assays show 3D DNA origami folding cooperatively in a structure-specific window of about 5 °C, foldable at constant temperature within it, and melting 5–10 °C higher within seconds while folding takes minutes to hours. Cooperativity spans connected subdomains; staple concentration and internal routing shift the window and the rate, routing by more than 100-fold at fixed shape and composition. A kinetic model, partly read, blames spurious short binding for low-temperature inhibition, and a short-domain design folds only when cooled fast to its folding temperature. | Read |
| [NOTE-1645](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1645.md) | Dannenberg et al. — Modelling DNA origami self-assembly at the domain level | A Gillespie-simulated domain-level model of one planar origami scaffold folding in constant excess staples, free energies from SantaLucia duplex terms, coaxial stacking and freely-jointed-chain loop entropy. The global version is a state function, the local one is path-dependent. Loop and stacking cooperativity sharpen the transition and produce hysteresis matching the scale seen by SYBR Green; faster cooling or fewer staples move annealing several times more than melting; cooperativity acts through neighbours, not distant staples. No misbinding, so no misfolds. | Read |
| [NOTE-1652](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1652.md) | Christie et al. — Genetic adaptation to captivity in a single generation of hatchery steelhead | A pedigree of 12,700 Hood River winter steelhead over 15 run-years tests two predictions that domestication selection makes and relaxed selection does not. First-generation hatchery fish spawned in the hatchery leave nearly twice as many returning offspring as wild fish spawned alike (4 of 5 run-years); and wild broodstock most successful in the hatchery leave offspring least successful in the wild (71% lower per capita for families of five or more returns; 7 of 8 run-years). Inbreeding cannot explain it and relaxed selection predicts a flat slope. The one exception year had few broodstock and smolts reared at low density. Less than one generation in captivity suffices. | Read |
| [NOTE-1657](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1657.md) | Morris et al. — global review of conservation translocations of terrestrial vertebrates | A global systematic review of 514 terrestrial-vertebrate translocations (1895–2017), read as its preprint, modelled on practitioner-calibrated success (n = 257) and generation-weighted population growth (n = 87). Numbers released matter most, with a plateau above about 20–50 individuals. On reported success, captive-bred and wild stock, and soft and hard release, look alike; on growth, captive-bred stock and soft release do worse. The authors suspect lenient success criteria among practitioners invested in captive breeding. Independence "without further augmentation" is the top rung of the outcome scale, and most reported successes did not reach it. Nothing on training, feeding after release, habituation or withdrawal of support. Resende et al. (2021), unread, report the opposite on soft release. | Read |
| [NOTE-1668](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1668.md) | Araki et al. — Fitness of hatchery-reared salmonids in the wild | A review of 14 studies of hatchery against wild salmonid fitness in the same habitat, nine on steelhead, and a quantitative-genetic model. Hatchery fish are generally less fit in the wild; nonlocal segregated stocks are worst (lifetime relative fitness 0.02–0.37); local wild broodstock helps but does not prevent the loss. In the authors' Hood River steelhead the loss is genetic and cumulative from the first to the second hatchery generation. Of the candidate mechanisms, relaxed selection is too slow and inbreeding would need to be too high; domestication selection is the most likely, and the model shows it can give a loss of more than 30% per generation on one trait only when selection is strong in both settings and heritability high, plausibly when it acts on several traits. | Read |
| [NOTE-1670](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1670.md) | Mussmann et al. — translocated greater prairie chickens and the perpetuation of conservation reliance | Illinois greater prairie chickens, rescued in the 1990s by translocated birds, re-examined twenty years on from 1831 shed feathers at six leks: small, declining, bottlenecked and inbred, with heterozygosity no different before and after translocation. The authors read the earlier rise as demographic expansion, not genetic rescue, and argue that supplying birds while the habitat threat persists perpetuates conservation reliance; reliance can fall below a threshold only if extrinsic and intrinsic causes are relieved together. The threshold is a conceptual figure, not a measurement. | Read |
| [NOTE-1672](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1672.md) | Underwood et al. — Hawai'i's endangered waterbirds held by perpetual wetland management | US Fish and Wildlife Service refuge biologists compare 1986–2007 population trends of three of Hawai'i's endangered waterbirds on six actively managed refuges with those on other wetlands, from semiannual statewide and monthly refuge counts. All three are stable or rising, and the refuges hold a share of each population more than twice their share of wetland. The upkeep is constant weed control, predator control and water management; an unmanaged marsh is the authors' example of what happens without it. They hold that management must be perpetual. The design has no unmanaged control. | Read |
| [NOTE-1674](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1674.md) | Brown et al. — Kirtland's Warbler viability after delisting, on supplied habitat | A 100-year full-annual-cycle simulation of the Kirtland's Warbler, a species recovered under management and proposed for delisting, whose breeding habitat is planted jack pine standing in for suppressed wildfire and whose recruitment is helped by cowbird removal. Under current management the population holds at about 2,500 males; cutting the supplied habitat lowers the plateau to about 1,900 or 1,300 males without extinction, while habitat loss combined with drier Bahamian winters drives most runs below 200 males. The authors conclude the species stays reliant on humans to keep its habitat. A model, with no scenario that ends the supply altogether. | Read |
| [NOTE-1687](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1687.md) | Grimshaw, Smyth and Stepanyants — Decay of Benjamin–Ono solitons under dissipation | A weakly damped Benjamin–Ono soliton stays a soliton whose amplitude slides down its one-parameter family at a rate set by an energy balance: exponentially under linear damping, twice as fast as a linear wave; algebraically under viscous, Landau, boundary-layer and Chezy losses; and to zero in a finite time under radiative loss, after which it becomes an envelope soliton. Where mass is not conserved a trailing shelf forms and the adiabatic theory eventually fails. Asymptotics checked against numerics; KdV laws quoted, not derived. | Read |
| [NOTE-1688](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1688.md) | Grelu and Akhmediev — Dissipative solitons for mode-locked lasers | A review by two of the concept's main authors. A conservative soliton balances nonlinearity against dispersion alone and is one of a family selected by the initial data; a dissipative soliton is a single attractor, its energy, profile and chirp fixed by the parameters, held by an exact gain–loss balance with continuous exchange and an internal energy flow. Bound states are robust, exploding solitons return to their shape, new solitons nucleate from noise above a fluctuation threshold, and cavity solitons are written and erased by a transient beam. No pump existence threshold, bistability or hysteresis is discussed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1689](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1689.md) | Zabusky and Porter — Soliton (Scholarpedia) | A solitary wave is held by a balance of nonlinearity and dispersion; a soliton keeps its shape at constant speed and comes out of a collision unchanged except for a phase shift, which in a conservative system means amplitude, shape and velocity are conserved. Zabusky and Kruskal named it in 1965 from numerical KdV solutions; inverse scattering explained it as integrability. Topological, dissipative and other relatives are only named, and in general lack the collision property. | Read |
| [NOTE-1691](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1691.md) | Zheng et al. — Nonlinear reshaping of Gaussian water wave packets | In a deep-water flume, Gaussian packets with the soliton's width disperse below its amplitude, travel nearly unchanged near it (over 1.07 dispersion lengths) and focus like a multi-soliton above it, as NLS and modified-NLS simulations predict. The long-time outcome, radiation or one or more solitons, is anticipated, not observed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1692](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1692.md) | Herr et al. — Temporal solitons in optical microresonators | First observation of temporal dissipative Kerr solitons in a microresonator. Sweeping a cw pump down in frequency over a resonance of a MgF2 resonator, onto the red-detuned lower branch, gives discrete steps in transmission; simulation and the approximate analytic Lugiato-Lefever soliton show each step is a state of N solitons, N falling step by step and varying between simulated scans with the random seeding. The solitons exist only for √3 < ζ0 < π²f²/8, have a shape fixed by resonator and pump, are held by the pump against cavity loss, persist until it is switched off, and make the red-detuned regime thermally self-stable. Hysteresis is not named, no reverse sweep is shown, no decay is measured, and no experimental statistics of N are given. | Read |
| [NOTE-1693](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1693.md) | Cui and Wang — Eigenvalues of the Zakharov–Shabat system | A Chebyshev–QR method for the discrete Zakharov–Shabat eigenvalues, which count the solitons an NLS initial profile forms, tested against Satsuma and Yajima's exact κn = i(A + 1/2 − n) for A sech x (1.8 sech x: two solitons). The paper states no formation threshold; A ≤ 1/2 forming none is the reader's derivation from the quoted formula. | Read |
| [NOTE-1694](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1694.md) v2 | Tong — TASI Lectures on Solitons | Read for the topological charge and the kinks. In each of Tong's four solitons, finite action or energy forces the fields to a vacuum at the boundary; the boundary maps fall into homotopy classes, which split configurations into sectors labelled by a charge measured as a surface term; and the action, energy or tension in a sector is bounded below by the charge, the bound saturated by first-order Bogomolny equations in theories whose couplings are tuned to critical, supersymmetric values. A domain wall, "or kink", interpolates between distinct isolated vacua at its two ends. Vortex-antivortex annihilation is assumed, "expected (at least for suitably slow collisions)". That such solitons end only by annihilation or at a boundary is the reader's inference, not Tong's sentence. | Read |
| [NOTE-1698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1698.md) v2 | Fodor — Radiation of oscillons | Read, Chapter 2 and the introduction and summary. The review derives, for a real scalar with a potential analytic at its minimum, that the sine-Gordon breathers are the only one-parameter family of exactly periodic localized solutions shrinking to the vacuum, and that small-amplitude oscillons radiate at a rate exponentially small in the amplitude parameter, by complex extension, matched asymptotics and Borel summation, checked by two independent calculations and against numerics. From the core energy, which scales as ε^(2−d), 3+1 dimensional oscillons are stable only above a minimum amplitude and suddenly decay below it, while small and moderate 1 and 2 dimensional ones are stable and never decay. That no isolated breather exists is stated and supported numerically, not derived; the leading radiation coefficient vanishes at isolated parameter values. Whether fine-tuned states are permanent is contested by Gleiser & Krackow (2019) and left unresolved. | Read |
| [NOTE-1699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1699.md) | Copeland, Gleiser and Müller — Oscillons | The paper that named oscillons. A spherically symmetric real scalar field in 3+1 dimensions with a double-well potential is evolved numerically from subcritical bubbles at rest. Inside a window of initial radius (Gaussian, about 2.4 to 4.5 m^-1) the bubble sheds energy and settles into a state of nearly constant radius and energy, independent of the initial radius, that radiates almost nothing for 10^3–10^4 m^-1 and then decays quickly. A one-degree-of-freedom ansatz explains the lower radius bound and the end, and virialization tracks which live longest. Simulation only, spherical symmetry only, stability tested only against radial perturbations, the upper radius bound unexplained, lifetimes read off an energy plateau. | Read |
| [NOTE-1701](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1701.md) | Alía and Esteban — Weaning from mechanical ventilation | A review by investigators of the Spanish weaning trials. About three quarters of patients can be extubated after one passed trial of spontaneous breathing, and immediate extubation then beats gradual withdrawal; 30 and 120 min trials, on T-tube or low pressure support, are equivalent. For those who fail, gradual withdrawal with rest while the causes are treated: once-daily T-tube trials or pressure support, SIMV worst. The abstract says the opposite of the body about SIMV. | Read |
| [NOTE-1702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1702.md) | Jaber et al. — Ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction in humans | A review by authors of one of the human biopsy studies. Fully controlled ventilation lowers diaphragm force within hours in animals, through oxidative stress, less protein synthesis and more proteolysis; human biopsies from brain-dead donors show the same atrophy, injury and markers, correlated with how long ventilation lasted, and twitch pressure in patients fell by about a third in six days. Keeping spontaneous effort lessens the loss in animals without abolishing it. Recovery after ventilation is unstudied. | Read |
| [NOTE-1703](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1703.md) | Broersen et al. — Adrenal insufficiency after corticosteroid use, a meta-analysis | A meta-analysis of 74 articles (136 study groups, 3,753 adult corticosteroid users) on biochemical adrenal insufficiency, the body's own cortisol production suppressed. The pooled share runs from 4.2% after nasal use to 52.2% after intra-articular use; in asthma it rises with dose and with duration; after stopping it recedes incompletely, to 14.9% at 4 weeks after short high-dose courses and 25.3% at 6 months after long medium-dose use. Cross-study strata with high risk of bias; the two retest groups differ in regimen and interval together, and Figure 4 mislabels the 6-month retest. | Read |
| [NOTE-1704](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1704.md) | Goligher et al. — Avoiding insufficient and excessive effort | A review by fourteen intensivists. Ventilation can harm the diaphragm at both ends of effort: atrophy when over-assistance or sedation suppresses effort, and possibly injury when effort is excessive, a hypothesis still to be confirmed. So ventilation and sedation should be titrated to keep an effort near that of quiet breathing, with bedside measures and target ranges given. Support proportional to the patient's own neural drive (NAVA) makes disuse from over-assistance unlikely. No new data; trials are awaited. | Read |
| [NOTE-1705](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1705.md) | Beuschlein et al. — The ESE and Endocrine Society guideline on glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency | A joint clinical guideline built on systematic reviews of recovery and of tapering. Supraphysiologic glucocorticoids invariably suppress the HPA axis; prolonged use brings pituitary hyporesponsiveness and, in rodents, adrenal atrophy; after withdrawal ACTH recovers first, then cortisol, over a few months to up to four years and incompletely in a minority. It recommends no taper under 3–4 weeks of use, and otherwise a taper fast at high doses and slow near the physiologic dose, keeping replacement low enough to leave a stimulus for recovery. The schedule is consensus: no study compared taper schemes. Its Table 6 mislabels Broersen et al.'s asthma strata as inhaled-only. | Read |
| [NOTE-1706](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1706.md) | Shah, Hart and Kaltsakas — Prolonged weaning | An educational review of weaning. Readiness is tested by a spontaneous breathing trial of 30 to 120 min, since predictors have low power; patients are classed simple, difficult or prolonged by how many trials fail or how long weaning takes, after the 2007 consensus. Clinicians underestimate readiness, and delay goes with failure. After failed or prolonged weaning outcomes are poor: half still ventilated at a year, and 42% of those liberated after prolonged weaning needing ventilation again. | Read |
| [NOTE-1727](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1727.md) | Kara and others (2011) — Fetal Cells Traffic to Injured Maternal Myocardium and Undergo Cardiac Differentiation | In a mouse model, wild-type virgin females mated with eGFP-transgenic males had a left anterior descending artery ligation (myocardial infarction) at gestation day 12. eGFP-tagged cells of fetal origin were then tracked in the mother. Fetal cells were enriched in injured hearts relative to sham and uninjured controls, located in infarct and peri-infarct zones, and by 3–4 weeks co-expressed markers of cardiomyocytes, smooth muscle and endothelium. Sorted fetal cells from maternal hearts expanded clonally in vitro and, on neonatal cardiomyocyte feeders, became spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes; mononuclearity and X/Y FISH argue against fusion. FACS across organs showed selective homing to the injured heart rather than to liver, lung or skeletal muscle, with heart counts rising after delivery. About 38–40% of the fetal cells in the maternal heart expressed Cdx2, a trophoblast-stem marker. The authors propose fetal-maternal stem-cell transfer as a maternal response to cardiac injury, motivated by the high recovery rate in peripartum cardiomyopathy. | Read |
| [NOTE-1728](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1728.md) | Kinder and others (2017) — Immunological implications of pregnancy-induced microchimerism | A review arguing that the bidirectional transfer of cells between mother and fetus during pregnancy, and their persistence for decades (fetal cells in mothers: fetal microchimerism, FMC; maternal cells in offspring: maternal microchimerism, MMC), is not accidental but serves reproductive fitness: in mice, maternal microchimeric cells sustain offspring's regulatory T cell tolerance of non-inherited maternal antigens (NIMAs), which protects the offspring's own later pregnancies sired by NIMA-matched males (Kinder et al. 2015, ref. 14), and fetal cells retained in mothers may analogously protect later pregnancies (supported in humans by partner-specific protection against preeclampsia). Microchimeric cells may also replace injured tissue or be targets of alloimmunity resembling autoimmunity; causal roles in humans are mostly unestablished. The authors propose redefining immunological identity to include a "microchiome" of familially relevant "extended-self" antigens. | Read |
| [NOTE-1730](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1730.md) | Hafer-Hahmann (2026) — The Evolution and Ecology of Host Manipulation in Helminth Parasites: A Phylogenetic Meta‐Analysis | A Bayesian phylogenetic meta-analysis (brms) of host manipulation by trophically transmitted helminths: 1,635 observations, 207 papers, 82 parasite and 80 host taxa. Effect size is Cohen's d for infected vs uninfected hosts, signed by assumed effect on predation susceptibility. Fixed effects: parasite stage, predator context, behaviour type, infection method, year, SE (for publication bias). Random effects: study, host and parasite phylogeny, host-parasite pair. It then tests candidate ecological and evolutionary drivers (host size, trophic level, longevity, parasite adult size, infection site, habitat, next-host type). | Read |
| [NOTE-1738](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1738.md) | Nakhal et al. (2026) — Maternal gut dysbiosis is associated with altered enteric and cortical inhibitory circuit development | Pregnant GAD67-GFP mice (6 control, 6 treated dams) received oral vancomycin (20 mg/kg/day, GD8–GD17) to induce gut dysbiosis. Dams' microbiota lost diversity (Chao1, Shannon; PERMANOVA R² = 0.77). In offspring at postnatal day 14 (12 pups per group), the authors report lower maternal–offspring microbial transmission fidelity, reduced body weight, crypt and muscularis thickness, fragmented Claudin-1, reduced myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus area without change in neuronal density, shorter and less branched GAD67+ interneurons in layers II/III of somatosensory and motor cortex (not medial entorhinal cortex or CA1), and lower interneuron density in motor cortex only. Correlations between offspring taxa and these phenotypes are reported. The authors repeatedly label the findings descriptive associations. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1756](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1756.md) | Cuny and Poelman (2022) — Evolution of koinobiont parasitoid host regulation and consequences for indirect plant defence | Koinobiont parasitoids let the host keep feeding while their larvae develop inside it, and regulate the host's growth: usually arresting it (smaller hosts eating less), sometimes prolonging it (larger hosts eating more), and some species switch with conditions. The regulation is done by injected and secreted factors, and it changes the plant's responses to the parasitized herbivore, so it reaches the wider community. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1758.md) | Jia and others 2026 — Neuron–tumor crosstalk in cancer: molecular mechanisms and translational advances | A narrative review of cancer neuroscience. Tumours recruit nerves (neurotrophins such as NGF and BDNF, axon-guidance cues, perineural invasion) or, in the brain, integrate into existing circuits through tumour–neuron synapses; nerve signalling, chiefly sympathetic norepinephrine through β-adrenergic receptors, then builds an immunosuppressive microenvironment; nerves also reach the tumour through endocrine and metabolic routes, including the transfer of mitochondria from neurons to cancer cells; and cancer pain feeds a loop that raises sympathetic tone. The authors name the whole pattern "tumor neuron hijack" and propose repurposed β-blockers, cholinergic drugs and neural-signal modulation, especially with immunotherapy. It reports no new data; most mechanisms it cites are preclinical. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1759](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1759.md) | Schepanski and others (2022) — Pregnancy-induced maternal microchimerism shapes neurodevelopment and behavior in mice | Maternal cells (maternal microchimeric cells, MMc) transfer to the fetus and seed the fetal brain, concentrating in prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. By scRNA-seq, brain MMc are mostly microglia, plus T, B, endothelial and neuron-like cells. Using a reciprocal Rag2−/−IL-2rγc−/− × wild-type mating that yields offspring with reduced MMc ("MMclow") against controls ("MMcpos"), and excluding maternal-immune-activation confounders, the authors show MMc reduction causes: excess microglial proliferation and hyperactivation, excess engulfment of presynaptic terminals (Vglut1+ significant), reduced neuronal branching, lower oscillatory power in prefrontal-hippocampal circuits, and behavioral deficits (altered ultrasonic vocalizations; impaired recognition memory). Adoptive transfer of wild-type immune cells into Rag2−/−IL-2rγc−/− dams at E12.5 ("MMclow+AT") restores MMc number, microglia number, pruning, oscillatory power and behavior. | Read |
| [NOTE-1763](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1763.md) | Cincinnati Children's — Deeper microchimerism study | A research-news post on Peng, Way and colleagues (Immunity, 2025): in mice, tolerance of non-inherited maternal antigens is sustained only by the small fraction of maternal microchimeric cells that co-express LysM and CD11c, and depleting that fraction erases the tolerance while most maternal cells persist. The post reads this as the persistence of foreign cells coming apart from their function, and as a puzzle about why the remaining cells are not rejected. | Read |
| [NOTE-1764](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1764.md) | Levin 2024/2025 — The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next‐Generation Biomedicine | Levin argues that biomedicine's bottom-up, molecular ("hardware") paradigm cannot achieve anatomical control (birth defects, regeneration, cancer, aging) and should be complemented by a top-down program that treats cells and tissues as an "agential material" with memories, goals and problem-solving competencies, i.e. a collective intelligence navigating anatomical, transcriptional and physiological spaces. Systems sit on a "spectrum of persuadability" (hardware rewiring → setpoint rewriting → training → reasoning with), and where a system sits is "not a philosophical question but an empirical one". Bioelectric networks (ion channels, gap junctions) are the "cognitive glue" that binds cells into larger collectives with larger goals, and the most tractable interface; existing ion-channel drugs can be repurposed as "electroceuticals". Cancer is read as cells' "cognitive light cone" shrinking: "cancer cells are not more selfish; they just have smaller selves", with gap-junction closure starting a feedback of dissociation. A roadmap follows: rewrite setpoints rather than force states (getting the system's "buy-in"), first/second/third-order interventions, patient-derived biobots, disease as learned attractors, and "eavesdropping" on tissues as sensors. The end-game is an "Anatomical Compiler". | Read |
| [NOTE-1766](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1766.md) | van Roosmalen & de Bekker (2024) — Mechanisms Underlying Ophiocordyceps Infection and Behavioral Manipulation of Ants: Unique or Ubiquitous? | Review of what is proposed about how Ophiocordyceps unilateralis s.l. infects carpenter ants and changes their behaviour (loss of daily rhythm, reduced communication with nestmates, hyperactivity, staggering, summiting, biting at about solar noon, death), compared with other behaviour-manipulating parasites (Entomophthora in flies, baculovirus in caterpillars, and others). Two hypothesised mechanism families: secreted fungal effectors (enterotoxins, an aflatrem-like alkaloid cluster, protein tyrosine phosphatases, juvenile-hormone modulation, small secreted proteins predicted to bind ant GPCRs), and disruption and resetting of the host's biological clock. Similar phenotypes and some genes across unrelated systems suggest convergent evolution. | Read |
| [NOTE-1767](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1767.md) | Ahmed and others (2022) — Microbiota-derived metabolites as drivers of gut–brain communication | A review of how gut-microbial metabolites (SCFAs, tryptophan/indole derivatives, bile acids, sulfated phenolics and others) influence brain functions through immune, neural and endocrine routes, arranged by neurological function, with a closing assessment of how far human evidence supports the preclinical picture. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1768](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1768.md) | Chua et al. — Key questions and challenges in microchimerism biology | An expert survey (29 researchers, 63 unique questions in seven themes) that states the field's settled points and open questions. Microchimeric cells are rare, persist for decades, cross into almost any tissue, and are tolerated partly by actively induced regulatory T cells; the depletion of one marked maternal subset removes tolerance without lowering total microchimerism. What they do, why they persist, and what counts as microchimerism are open. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1770](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1770.md) | Strand and Burke (2012) — Polydnaviruses as Symbionts and Gene Delivery Systems | Polydnaviruses (PDVs) are viruses carried by parasitoid wasps. In bracoviruses the provirus sits in every wasp cell; it replicates only in calyx cells of the female ovary, and the virions are injected with the eggs into a caterpillar host, where their genes are expressed but never replicate. The genome has two parts in different places in the wasp genome: core replication genes (inherited from a nudivirus ancestor, vertically transmitted, never packaged) and packaged DNA segments carrying virulence genes that immunosuppress the host and alter its growth. Ichnoviruses have similar life cycles but no shared core genes: convergence. | Read |
| [NOTE-1772](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1772.md) | George and Bates (2022) — Mechanisms Underlying Influence of Bioelectricity in Development | A review of how ion channels and membrane potential (Vmem) act in development: human channelopathies with developmental phenotypes, conserved roles across species, spontaneous calcium oscillations in non-excitable tissue, and the cellular processes (death, proliferation, polarity, migration) and signalling pathways (BMP, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog) that channels touch. It proposes calcium as the main mediator and a model in which Vmem and calcium oscillations, shaped by mechanical forces, coordinate cells across a tissue. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1773](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1773.md) | Almarzooqi and others (2026) — From association to causality: mechanistic pathways linking the gut microbiome to psychiatric disorders | A narrative review of the microbiota–gut–brain axis (MGBA) in psychiatry, organized around the move "from association to causality". It sets out a graded hierarchy of causal evidence (confounder-controlled association, temporal precedence, experimental necessity/sufficiency, human genetic or interventional validation, cross-cohort replication), reviews mechanisms (immune, HPA, vagal/ENS, barrier), grades the evidence per disorder, and reviews translation (psychobiotics, diet, FMT, biomarkers). Its verdict: the microbiome is "a biologically plausible and modifiable contributor within a complex, bidirectional system rather than a primary cause"; MDD has "moderate causal involvement"; anxiety and BD weaker; SCZ a disease modifier. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1775](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1775.md) | Sullivan, Dulac and others (2025 preprint) — Brain-immune interactions generate pathogen-specific sickness states | In mice, five sterile immune challenges modelling bacterial infection (LPS), viral infection (poly I:C), parasite infection (soluble *Toxoplasma* antigen, STAg), allergy (bee-venom PLA2) and colitis (DSS) produce distinct "sickness states" at three scales: organismal (temperature, food intake, locomotion, metabolism, social behaviour, ultrasonic vocalizations), cellular (whole-brain FOS activity, which a classifier uses to predict the challenge) and molecular (a 940-gene MERFISH atlas of the preoptic and paraventricular hypothalamus). The states cluster: LPS with poly I:C; STAg with DSS; PLA2 apart. STAg and DSS unexpectedly *increased* social interaction and activated hypothalamic "isolation" neurons that promote social drive. The authors conclude the brain, like the immune system, represents pathogen classes specifically. | Read |
| [NOTE-1781](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1781.md) | Boddy and others (2015) — Fetal microchimerism and maternal health: A review and evolutionary analysis of cooperation and conflict beyond the womb | An evolutionary (cooperation-and-conflict) framework for fetal microchimerism. Fetal cells cross into the mother, persist for decades, and have paradoxical associations with maternal health (both protective and harmful). The authors explain the paradox as a mix of aligned and conflicting fitness interests: fetal cells may aid maternal somatic maintenance (wound healing, stem-cell niche) where that is cheap to the offspring, and may manipulate maternal tissues (breast, thyroid, brain) to raise resource transfer above the maternal optimum, provoking maternal immune countermeasures and possible conflict escalation. They extend maternal-fetal conflict theory "beyond the womb" and offer testable predictions (Table 3) across lactation, thyroid, attachment, cancer, autoimmunity, and pregnancy signaling. | Read |
| [NOTE-1785](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1785.md) | Mpakosi and others (2024) — Deciphering the Role of Maternal Microchimerism in Offspring Autoimmunity: A Narrative Review | A narrative review of maternal-to-offspring microchimerism (MMc). Cells cross the placenta both ways; maternal cells enter the fetus from the second trimester and persist into adulthood. They include T cells, B and NK cells, monocytes and haematopoietic and mesenchymal progenitors; levels depend on HLA compatibility, PAPP-A and possibly delivery mode; MMc may pass across generations (grandmother, siblings). Protective roles: immune maturation, early-life infection defence, possibly transfer of pathogen-specific T-cell memory, tolerance to non-inherited maternal antigens via MSCs. Harmful associations: type 1 diabetes, neonatal lupus, juvenile myopathies, Sjögren's and others (no association with coeliac disease). The authors conclude the role remains unclear and the evidence is hampered by detection limits, small samples and non-standard methods. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1791](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1791.md) | Castela and others (2017) — Ccl2/Ccr2 signalling recruits a distinct fetal microchimeric population that rescues delayed maternal wound healing | Fetal microchimeric cells (FMCs) traffic into maternal circulation and persist for decades; on maternal injury they migrate to the site and aid repair. Here, in mice, a reparative FMC subset is CD11b+ CD34+ CD31+ (fetal "MPCs") and highly expresses CCR2. Its ligand CCL2 (secreted early by wound monocytes/endothelial cells) recruits these fetal cells to maternal skin wounds, where they transdifferentiate into endothelial cells and stimulate angiogenesis via Cxcl1. Low-dose CCL2 improves delayed wound healing in pregnant and post-partum (early and 6-month) mice but never in virgins, and the effect is CCR2-dependent (shown with Ccr2KO crosses). | Read |
| [NOTE-1801](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1801.md) | Reisinger and Cederroth (2026) — FDA Approval of the Congenital OTOF Gene Therapy Otarmeni Reshapes the Future of Hearing Loss Treatment | Comments on the FDA's approval (announced 23 April 2026) of Regeneron's Otarmeni, the first gene therapy for a genetic hearing loss (DFNB9, OTOF), and on convergent results from other programmes. Because the therapy is gene-specific and time-sensitive, infants with bilateral hearing loss need genetic diagnosis; clinical sequences should change so that children with profound loss and intact otoacoustic emissions get a genetic diagnosis before a cochlear implant. Outcomes are incomplete: a quarter of the CHORD trial children reached normal pure-tone sensitivity; others average 40–50 dB HL, possibly from incomplete transduction and unrestorable synapse loss; speech-in-noise, listening effort and fatigue need assessment. It calls for equitable access (Regeneron's free US provision; uncertain in Europe), a European rare-disorders network and registry with core outcomes, and attention to the Deaf community. | Read |
| [NOTE-1840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1840.md) | Fang, Jian, Li and Ma — AI-Newton: A Concept-Driven Physical Law Discovery System without Prior Physical Knowledge | AI-Newton discovers general physical laws from simulated noisy data across 46 classical-mechanics experiments without prior physical concepts. It keeps an experiment base and a theory base of symbols, concepts and laws written in a physical domain-specific language. Concepts are defined explicitly: dynamical (e.g. velocity as a derivative), intrinsic (e.g. mass, defined by the measurement procedure of a named experiment), and universal constants. | Read |
| [NOTE-1870](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1870.md) | Bragg et al. — AstaBench: Rigorous Benchmarking of AI Agents with a Scientific Research Suite | The paper argues that existing agent benchmark suites lack standard reproducible tools, ignore confounders (cost, tool access), lack standard task interfaces for general agents, lack tasks drawn from real product use, and lack comprehensive baselines. It sets out five principles and builds AstaBench to meet them: 11 benchmarks and 2,400+ problems in four categories, namely literature understanding, code and execution, data analysis, and end-to-end discovery. Alongside come a reproducible literature-search environment with date cut-offs (Asta Scientific Corpus), a cost-accounting toolkit and leaderboard (agent-eval), and an agent-baselines suite. | Skimmed |
